## Your dashboards are lying to you

At 2:14 a.m. the pager goes off. CPU, fine. Memory, fine. Error rate flat. Every dashboard you built is green, and checkout is still broken for 3% of users — the 3% routed through one bad pod in eu-west.

That gap, between "all my metrics look normal" and "the system is not working," is what observability closes.

The distinction from monitoring is worth being pedantic about, because teams spend real money getting it wrong. Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance. You knew disk could fill, so you graphed disk. Observability is the ability to answer questions you didn't think of, after the incident has already started, without shipping new code to collect the data. It's a property of your system, not a product you buy.

The failure modes have changed, too. A monolith fails loudly. Distributed systems fail in slivers: one slow dependency, one poisoned cache key, one customer whose payload is 40x bigger than anyone else's. Averages hide all of it. Your users live at p99.

The payoff isn't only faster incident response, though a team that can trace a request end to end spends less of the outage just locating the problem. It's that engineers stop guessing. They stop redeploying with print statements wedged in. They stop the ritual where four people join a call and take turns proposing theories nobody can test.

---

## Your dashboards are lying to you

At 2:14 a.m. the pager goes off. CPU is fine. Memory is fine. Five green dashboards insist the system is healthy, and meanwhile checkout is failing for something like three percent of users, and nobody on the call can say which three percent, or why.

Then the next incident arrives wearing a different mask, the logs are the wrong logs, and the cycle repeats. What breaks isn't the software. It's the team's ability to reason about the software it already shipped.

This post is about closing that gap on purpose, before the pager makes the decision for you.

## Nobody Knows Why Checkout Got Slow

Your p99 on `/checkout` went from 180 ms to four seconds sometime between Tuesday and Friday. That much you can see on the latency graph. Everything after that is guesswork.

So the team starts the ritual. Someone scrolls Grafana looking for a spike that lines up. Someone else pulls the deploy log and finds eleven releases in that window, any of which could be it. A third person opens the database dashboard, sees connection counts that look vaguely high, and says "maybe it's the pool?" — and now three engineers spend a day chasing a hypothesis that nobody can confirm or kill, because the data to settle it was never collected in the first place.

That's the actual cost. Not the outage. The hours your best people spend reconstructing what the system was doing, from evidence that wasn't designed to answer questions.

Monitoring tells you a thing broke. You picked the metric in advance, you set the threshold in advance, and the alert fires when the number crosses it. That works fine for the failures you predicted. It does nothing for the ones you didn't, which is most of them, because distributed systems fail in combinations nobody wrote a dashboard for.

Observability is the other move. You instrument richly enough that you can ask a question you never anticipated and get an answer in minutes. Which customer. Which shard. Which code path. Not "is it broken" but "what exactly is it doing right now."

**The Second Year Is the Hard One: What We Learned Breaking Up a Rails Monolith**

We split our monolith into 14 services. Eighteen months later we merged four of them back.

This talk is about what the migration diagrams leave out. The first extraction always goes fine — you pick a bounded context with clean edges, stand it up, cut traffic over, and everyone claps. Then you reach the parts of the codebase nobody understands: the joins that cross five tables, the billing flow that touches everything. That's where the schedule dies.

# A year remote: what we got wrong

We went remote in March, and the first thing we lost was the thing nobody had written down.

Our onboarding was never a document. It was a new hire sitting near someone for three weeks, overhearing why we don't touch the billing service on Fridays. Remote, that channel closed. Our fourth-month hire shipped nothing meaningful until August, and it wasn't their fault. We had never written the rules they were supposed to absorb. So we wrote them. What did break was the twenty-minute conversation that used to happen because two people got coffee at the same time. We haven't solved that. We fly everyone in for four days a quarter, which helps for maybe three weeks afterward.

# Case study: Brightwell Logistics

Brightwell Logistics runs freight-tracking software for about 400 regional carriers. Until early 2024, its engineers shipped on a fixed calendar: one release every three weeks, cut on a Tuesday, deployed Thursday night, with two people on call watching the rollout until midnight.

The cadence was not the real problem. The problem was what it did to the work in between. Changes piled up behind the release cut, so any failure meant bisecting three weeks of commits. Engineers batched risky changes with safe ones because there was no cheap way to ship a single fix.

Brightwell moved to Conveyor in March 2024. The first six weeks were mostly unglamorous plumbing: consolidating four CI configurations into one, adding health checks to services that had never had them, and writing rollback steps for the two databases nobody wanted to touch.

A year later:

- Deploys went from roughly 17 a year to four or five a week.
- Median time from merge to production fell from 11 days to under an hour.
- Change failure rate rose a little, 3% to 4%. Mean time to recovery dropped from six hours to 22 minutes.

"We expected the deploy count to go up," said Dana Okafor, VP of Engineering. "What surprised us was the arguments that stopped happening. Nobody negotiates for a slot in the release train anymore."

Brightwell still cuts a coordinated release for schema migrations, and still freezes deploys during peak shipping weeks in December. Everything else goes out when it is ready.

We have paid that six weeks something like fourteen times in the last year. That is most of an engineer-decade spent re-deriving decisions we already made.

The bet is that we stop paying it. By the end of the second year, a team should be able to go from an empty repo to production traffic in under a day, on paved defaults that already carry logging, tracing, secrets, rollback, and a working on-call rotation. Not because someone wrote a wiki page about how to do it, but because the path of least resistance does it for them.

That means treating the platform as a product with real users — our own engineers — and holding it to the same bar. It has a roadmap. It has SLOs. It can be abandoned for something better if it fails to earn its keep.

We are explicit about the cost. Roughly 15% of engineering capacity moves to platform work, and product roadmaps get slower for the first three quarters. We think that trade pays back sometime in year two and compounds after. If it doesn't, the metrics below will say so, and we'll unwind it.

## Vision

Two years from now, a team at this company should be able to take a service from empty repo to production traffic in under a week, without filing a ticket, without reading four conflicting runbooks, and without learning the deployment history of the last six years.

That is not where we are. Today the path to production runs through three deployment systems, two of which we keep alive only because a handful of critical services never migrated off them. Every new team pays a tax of roughly a month before they ship anything a customer sees, and most of that month is spent rediscovering things other teams already know. The tax is invisible in our roadmaps because it is charged to product teams, one at a time, in small amounts.

Platform work is how we stop charging it. The goal is a single supported path: one way to deploy, one way to get a database, one way to see what your service is doing at 3am. Not every possible need served, but the common ninety percent served well enough that stepping off the path becomes a deliberate choice with a written reason.

We measure this in time, not adoption. Time from first commit to first production request. Time from a page firing to an engineer knowing which service caused it. Time from a security patch landing upstream to it running everywhere. If those numbers fall by half over eight quarters, the investment paid for itself, and the argument for the next one makes itself.

## Vision

Two years out, a new service should reach production in a day, not a quarter.

That's the bet. Right now an engineer starting something new spends most of the first month on work nobody asked for: wiring auth, copying a CI config from whichever repo looked least stale, guessing at dashboards, filing a ticket to get a database. Median time from empty repo to first customer traffic is 34 days. About 60% of that is plumbing eleven other teams have already built eleven other ways.

We want to make that plumbing boring and mostly invisible. One paved path, owned by a team whose job is the path itself, with the escape hatches documented so that leaving the path is a decision rather than an accident. Product teams keep the parts that differentiate us and stop re-litigating the parts that don't.

This is a real trade. Platform work does not ship features, and for the first three or four quarters it will look like we slowed down. Some teams will lose autonomy they currently enjoy, including a few who use it well. We're accepting that because the alternative compounds against us: every quarter we defer this, the divergence between services grows and the eventual migration gets more expensive.

The measure we'll hold ourselves to is time-to-production for a greenfield service, tracked quarterly, with a target of under two days by the end of FY28. If that number isn't moving by the halfway mark, the strategy is wrong and we should say so.
